biggestGap: The pale army has grain now but still no PIGMENT: its stone carries zero rust-ochre staining, so where the film's limestone mottles from cool grey right up into warm rust — pale-stone warm/cool balance running p50 -0.13 to a p95 of +0.03, spread 0.26-0.31 — our pale pawns sit at p50 -0.287 with a p95 of -0.185, never once reaching even neutral. critiqueDetail:
What has genuinely improved, and it should be said plainly. Round 3's charge that the dark king's cape was 'a single glassy sheet with no mail grain' is answered: brightened crops of the right-hand caped figure now show a real repeating mail pattern — regular linked diamonds running in rows across the whole cape — and the pale pawn helm at frame bottom-left now carries a legible cross-shaped visor slit, which is exactly the crusader-helm detail the brief asks for. gradientAnisotropy has moved 1.116 -> 1.952 against the reference's 1.982, essentially matched, meaning edge energy is finally organised into oriented families rather than isotropic mush. I flag one honesty caveat on that number: much of the new orientation may be the chamber team's new vertical pier/screen streaks filling my background, not my mail rows, so I am not banking the whole gain for pieces.

What has not improved. The round-3 headline is not closed. Staining is still completely absent, and this round I measured it rather than eyeballing it. Sampling only stone-lit pixels (luminance 0.10-0.95) and computing an exposure-independent warm/cool balance (R-B)/(R+B): film pale pawn+plinth p05 -0.275 / p50 -0.126 / p95 +0.031, spread 0.306; film pale knight body spread 0.259; film pale bishop spread 0.219. Our cleanest pale pawn returns p05 -0.348 / p50 -0.287 / p95 -0.185, spread 0.163 — half the film's variation, and the entire distribution sits a full 0.16 colder. The one render sample that looks wider (pale pawn right, spread 0.222) only gets there because an orange flame is spilling on it; that is warmth in the LIGHT, not in the albedo, which is precisely the inversion I called out last round and it is unchanged. Side-by-side crops make it unarguable: the film's crouching pawn and its stepped plinth are covered in rust-brown blotches with hard irregular edges, dirt collected in every recess, chipped arrises; ours is an evenly toned blue-grey shell.

Surface incident overall went slightly backwards, not forwards. detailTotal 0.00508 vs the film's 0.01807 — a 3.6x deficit, marginally worse than round 3's 3.3x. detailByBand [0.00268, 0.00606, 0.00655] against [0.00872, 0.02218, 0.02350]: mid and coarse are unmoved from round 3 to three decimal places, and the FINE band actually regressed, 0.00402 -> 0.00268 (now 0.31x the film). On shape, normalising each to its coarse band, ours runs [0.40, 0.90, 1.00] and the film [0.37, 0.94, 1.00] — so the distribution across scales is close to correct and I will not repeat round 3's claim that it is misallocated. The deficit is now uniform: roughly 3.6x too little incident at every scale simultaneously. That is the signature of real carving being present in outline but nothing living on top of it — no pitting, no stain boundaries, no tool marks, no chipped edges. Fine band is where staining edges and chisel texture would land, and it is the band that got worse.

Context I am deliberately not making my headline, because it belongs to camera and lighting. The frame is a near-black void: medianLuminance 0.051 vs 0.106, fracShadow 0.765 vs 0.537 (worse than round 3's 0.7055), histogramEntropy 5.609 vs 6.861. The palette remains inverted and the cool balance has degraded — meanLitHueDeg 22.2 vs 212 (delta -189.8), warmFraction 0.1751 vs 0.0031, coolFraction 0.0848 vs 0.5181 (down from round 3's 0.1949), fracBlown 0.0183 vs the reference's exact 0.0000, driven by two blown orange flames that own the frame. The nominal subject — a mounted knight with conical cross-slit helm, chainmail cape and curved blade — is again not in shot. I had to brighten crops 3x before I could assess my own work at all. The piece team should understand that even perfectly stained limestone is invisible under this exposure, but the staining is missing on its own merits and would still be missing if the lights came up.

One unambiguous next move: paint irregular rust-ochre blotching into the pale army's ALBEDO — hard-edged, high-frequency, mask-driven, concentrated in mouldings, recesses and plinth steps, covering roughly a third of each pale surface, warm enough that it survives the cold grade and pulls the stone's warm/cool p95 from -0.185 up to about 0.00. Do it in the material, not in the light.

history.gap: The pieces have no figurative geometry at all — every foreground chessman is a featureless tapered low-poly cone with visible flat-shaded facets, where the film frame shows armoured riders on rearing horses with cross-slit conical helms and curved sabres, crouching domed-helm pawns, and a huge draped chainmail cape, each on a hexagonal stepped moulded plinth.

The chessmen have silhouettes now but no SKIN: the pale army is uniform clean cold white with none of the film's irregular rust-ochre blotching, and every helm, torso, cape and shield is a smooth unbroken surface with zero carved incident (brow ridges, mail rings, shield rims and bosses, tabard/drapery folds, tooled chisel texture) — so mid-band detail sits at 0.0061 against the film's 0.0222, and each piece reads as an unfinished clay maquette rather than carved, stained limestone.

Every pale piece and plinth in the film is blotched over a third of its surface with hard-edged irregular orange-brown patches that pool in the mouldings and streak down the plinth steps; ours are uniform clean blue-grey stone from helm to base.
